terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. `node src/orders.ts` runs the order code, and `npm run types` checks its types.

tasks.title: Name the shape of an order line
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/orders.ts`, `lineGrams` and `lineLabel` take the same shape written out twice, and the second copy is out of date. Write a type alias called `Line`, with `export` in front: an object with `blend` (text), `tins` (a number) and `gramsPerTin` (a number). Use `Line` as the type of the parameter of both functions. Leave their bodies and result types as they are.

Check reads both functions for `Line` in their parameters and for their result types. It compiles code of its own: a `Line` passed to both functions must compile, while a `Line` with a property missing or of the wrong type, or a line without its grams per tin passed to `lineLabel`, must be refused. It calls both functions with lines of its own.
nextSteps: Run `npm run types` and read the error for `lineLabel`: which property does its copy of the shape not have?
Write the type alias above the two functions: `export type`, the name, `=` and the object type.
Replace both written-out object types with the name.
hints: `Property 'gramsPerTin' does not exist on type '{ blend: string; tins: number; }'` means the shape written on `lineLabel` has only two properties. Writing the shape once, with a name, keeps the copies from drifting apart.
A type alias is the word `type`, a name, `=` and any type, here an object type with all three properties. After that, the name can go wherever a type goes.
`export type Line = { blend: string; tins: number; gramsPerTin: number }`, then `line: Line` in both parameter lists.

tasks.title: Write a customer as an interface
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write an interface called `Customer`, with `export` in front: `name` (text), `email` (text) and `phone` (text), which a customer may leave out. Use `Customer` as the type of the parameter of `contactLine` and of `firstCustomer`, and write the result type of `contactLine`. Leave the body of `contactLine` as it is.

Check reads your lines for the word `interface` in front of `Customer`, for `Customer` on `contactLine` and `firstCustomer`, and for the result type. It compiles code of its own: customers with and without a phone number must compile, while a customer without an email, a phone number that is a number, a contact line used as a number or a property `firstCustomer` does not have must be refused. It calls `contactLine` with customers of its own.
nextSteps: Write the interface above `contactLine`: `export interface`, the name and the properties in curly braces.
Mark the phone number as a property a customer may leave out.
Put the name after the parameter of `contactLine` and after `firstCustomer`, and write the result type.
hints: An interface names an object shape, like a type alias does, but it is written without `=`: the word `interface`, the name and the curly braces.
A question mark after a property's name makes it one an object may leave out, the same as in the object types of the last issue.
`export interface Customer { name: string; email: string; phone?: string }`, then `customer: Customer`, `): string` and `firstCustomer: Customer`.

tasks.title: Put an address inside a parcel
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a type called `Address`: `name`, `street`, `town` and `postcode`, all text. Then write a type called `Parcel`: `orderId` (text), `grams` (a number) and `to`, an `Address`. Use `Address` by its name inside `Parcel`, and put `export` in front of both. Then use `Parcel` as the type of the parameter of `shipTo`, and write its result type. Either a type alias or an interface is fine for each.

Check reads your lines for `Address` inside `Parcel`, for `Parcel` on `shipTo` and for its result type. It compiles code of its own: a parcel with an address, its town read as text and its address used as an `Address`, which must compile, and an address without a postcode, an address written as one line of text, grams as text or a parcel without an address, which must be refused. It calls `shipTo` with a parcel of its own.
nextSteps: Write `Address` first, with its four properties.
Write `Parcel` under it, and give `to` the type `Address`.
Use `Parcel` on the parameter of `shipTo`, and write its result type.
hints: A property's type can be any type, and that includes a name you wrote yourself.
Write `Address` before `Parcel`, so it reads in order. Then in `Parcel`, `to` gets the type `Address`, just as `grams` gets `number`.
`export type Parcel = { orderId: string; grams: number; to: Address }`, and `shipTo(parcel: Parcel): string`.

tasks.title: Build batch tins on tins
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a type called `BatchTin`, with `export` in front: everything a `Tin` has, and `batch` (a number) as well. Build it on the `Tin` above it instead of writing its properties out again, with either form the lesson shows. Leave `Tin` as it is. Then write a function called `batchLabel`, with `export` in front, from the word `function` to its closing brace. It takes a `BatchTin` and gives back text like `'Ember Oolong, 100 g, batch 3'`. Write its result type, then take away the `//` in front of the line at the end, to see it run.

Check reads your lines for `Tin` in `BatchTin` and for the result type of `batchLabel`. It compiles code of its own: a plain tin, a batch tin, a batch tin used as a tin and its label as text must compile, while a batch tin without its batch or its grams, a batch as text, a plain tin passed to `batchLabel` or a label used as a number must be refused. It calls `batchLabel` with tins of its own.
nextSteps: Pick one of the two ways the lesson shows to build one shape on another.
Write `BatchTin` under `Tin`, with only the batch number written out.
Write `batchLabel` whole, with its parameter type and result type.
Take away the `//` in front of the last line, and run both commands.
hints: Writing `blend` and `grams` out again would work today, but when `Tin` gets a new property, `BatchTin` would not. Building on `Tin` keeps them together.
An interface can say `extends` and the name of the shape it builds on. A type alias can join two shapes with `&`.
`export interface BatchTin extends Tin { batch: number }`, then `export function batchLabel(tin: BatchTin): string {` and a template literal.
